title: NASA's Curiosity Rover Photographs a Vast 'Sea of Polygons' on Mars That 'Took Our Breath Away'
excerpt: The rover discovered the largest field of honeycomb-like fracture patterns ever found on Mars while exploring Valle Grande, offering new clues about the planet's ancient watery past.
body:
• NASA's Curiosity rover discovered a massive field of honeycomb-shaped polygonal fractures while exploring Mars's Valle Grande valley.
  • The formations are the largest of their kind ever found on Mars, stretching as far as the rover's cameras can image.
  • Scientists believe the patterns may have formed billions of years ago when water repeatedly soaked and dried the ground.
  • Each polygon measures roughly 4 to 8 centimeters across, and the structures were found on both flat terrain and the sides of a 6-meter butte.

NASA's Curiosity rover has stumbled upon the largest field of honeycomb-shaped patterns ever found on Mars, a discovery that scientists say could unlock new details about the planet's ancient relationship with water.

The formations, known as polygonal fractures, were spotted as the rover explored a valley called Valle Grande in Gale Crater. While Curiosity has encountered small patches of similar patterns before, the scale of this discovery is unprecedented — the honeycomb-like structures stretch across the landscape as far as the rover's cameras can see.

"We've seen a lot of fascinating landscapes through Curiosity's eyes, but this sea of polygons took our breath away."

— Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity Project Scientist, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory

A Giant Martian Honeycomb

The 360-degree panorama captured on July 19 and 20 reveals polygonal crack patterns blanketing the terrain. Each polygon measures roughly 4 to 8 centimeters (1.5 to 3 inches) across, according to NASA. The rover even found the structures extending up the sides of a 6-meter (20-foot) butte nicknamed "Miraflores."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KmikAcU3GvY

"We measured their shapes and chemistry carefully and are hopeful there are clues in the data as to how these features formed," Vasavada said.

The team had earlier driven Curiosity toward an area that appeared lighter in tone when viewed from orbit and relatively smooth from the rover's earlier vantage points. What they found instead was a terrain covered in the distinctive geometric patterns.

"Reaching this unit, the rover team was surprised to see the unit covered with polygonal structures like the top of a giant Martian honeycomb," NASA said in an update.

Clues to Mars's Watery Past

Scientists are not yet certain how the polygons formed, but the leading hypothesis involves water. Similar patterns on Earth are left behind when lakes dry out and sediment cracks in repeating geometric shapes. The process often occurs in areas that have been dried out and rehydrated in multiple cycles.

If that interpretation holds, the Valle Grande polygons would provide further evidence that parts of Mars experienced extended periods of wet-dry cycling billions of years ago — conditions that some astrobiologists consider favorable for the emergence of simple life forms.

Curiosity has been exploring Mars since landing in Gale Crater in 2012. Over nearly 14 years, the rover has found evidence that the crater once contained a lake system with the right chemical ingredients and nutrients to potentially support microscopic life.

Alongside the Polygons: A Geological Puzzle

The area surrounding the polygonal structures was strewn with small, dark-toned rocks that present their own mystery. Because Mars has a much thinner atmosphere than Earth, meteorites strike its surface far more frequently, and some of these dark rocks may be fragments ejected by distant impacts.

"Examination of some previous dark 'float' rocks indicated the presence of nickel, common in meteorites but less so in Martian rocks," the team noted. "But are all of the dark-toned pebbles and cobbles meteorites? Further investigations should help."

An Aging Rover With Miles to Go

The discovery comes even as Curiosity shows its age. Recent photos of the rover reveal extensive damage to one of its six aluminum wheels, with large sections of the outer casing broken away. NASA has managed the issue by selecting smoother terrain and updating the rover's traction-control software, but engineers are also preparing contingency procedures to shed the damaged wheel section if necessary.

For now, the plucky rover continues to deliver surprises. Its latest find adds to a remarkable portfolio of discoveries about ancient Mars — and a reminder that even after more than a decade, the planet still has secrets worth crossing millions of miles to uncover.
